title: Workplace mental toll tipped to hit $27bn
full_text:
The cost to the national economy of workplace mental ill-health would more than double to $27bn a year by 2042 without corrective action, with lost productivity accounting for more than half the direct cost, a new report finds.
Research by Mentally Healthy Workplaces Australia found workplace mental health issues were currently costing the economy $12bn a year in lost GDP, equivalent to $436 per person per year, and would jump by 125 per cent over the next 15 years if no action was taken.
According to the research, the inclusion of substantially reduced tax revenue and higher income support payments would add an extra 15 per cent in costs, wiping an additional $1.8bn from the economy.
MHWA is convened by Monash University as a consortium of industry, unions, governments and regulators, insurers, technologists, service providers, investors and researchers. The centre has received an initial $12m in funding, including $5.4m from the NSW government and $4.5m from the Victorian government.
The MHWA research found workplace-driven mental ill-health was a leading contributor to the slowdown in productivity.
Lost productivity due to absenteeism, presenteeism (working while unwell), staff turnover and lower workforce participation accounted for about 54 per cent of direct economic costs, Professor Margo Lydon, executive director and co-lead at MHWA, said the cost of lost productivity was initially borne by employers before shifting into workers’ compensation, life and health insurance, and government-funded support systems.
“Workplace-driven mental ill-health is not a future issue – it is a social and financial crisis that is already imposing substantial and rapidly growing burdens on Australia’s economy and workplaces,” Professor Lydon said.
She said structural shifts in the labour market, including automation and the rise of artificial intelligence, would only intensify psychosocial pressures on workers, making a nationally co-ordinated, prevention-led response even more urgent.
“Without such a response, costs will only continue to grow for governments, employers, workplace regulators, insurers, individuals, and the broader community,” she said.
The research came as Safe Work Australia called for a dedicated national approach to reduce work-related death and better mechanisms to ensure coronial findings were shared, assessed and acted on.
Releasing a review of model work health and safety laws, SWA said AI, climate change and harmful workplace conduct, including work-related violence and harassment, were the three major challenges reshaping workplaces and creating new or intensified WHS risks. The union movement highlighted the SWA call for a national strategy on AI and emerging technologies to address risks from workplace surveillance, work allocation, intensity and reduced worker control, as well as a recommended national workplace safety strategy on climate change.
